questions.question: Cisco SD-Access overlay control plane separates a device's IDENTITY (its IPv4/IPv6 address as seen by apps) from its LOCATION (the routing locator — the fabric edge node attached to). The mapping is kept in a control-plane database. Endpoints can move between fabric edges without renumbering. Which protocol provides this control plane?
options: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) with Map-Server/Resolver
VXLAN encapsulation acting as the SD-Access control plane
OMP, Cisco SD-WAN's Overlay Management Protocol for vSmart
IS-IS running between fabric nodes in the SD-Access underlay
questions.explanation: LISP is the SD-Access control plane: EIDs (Endpoint Identifiers — host IP/MAC) are mapped to RLOCs (Routing Locators — fabric edge IPs) by Map-Server/Map-Resolver nodes, so endpoints can roam between edges without renumbering. VXLAN is the DATA plane that encapsulates user traffic — it does not maintain the EID/RLOC database. OMP is the route-distribution protocol used by Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela), not by SD-Access. IS-IS runs in the SD-Access underlay to provide IP reachability between fabric nodes, but the endpoint identity-to-location mapping lives in LISP, not in the IGP.

questions.question: A data centre needs Layer-2 reachability across racks AND beyond the 4094 VLAN limit. The team picks an L2-over-L3 overlay that encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789), uses a 24-bit VNI (~16M segments), and is routed by the underlay. Which encapsulation?
options: GENEVE (IETF flexible NVO encapsulation over UDP 6081)
VXLAN with a 24-bit VNI carried over UDP 4789
NVGRE (Microsoft GRE-based overlay with a 24-bit VSID)
STT (VMware Stateless Transport Tunnelling using TCP segmentation offload)
questions.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet in UDP destined to port 4789 and tags each segment with a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier — ~16 million segments versus the 4094-VLAN limit — and is the de-facto overlay in Cisco SD-Access and ACI. GENEVE solves a similar problem but uses UDP 6081 and a variable TLV-based header, not the fixed VXLAN format. NVGRE is Microsoft's competing GRE-based overlay (no UDP, uses GRE protocol 47). STT is VMware's TCP-shaped overlay that has been largely superseded by GENEVE — neither matches the UDP-4789 / 24-bit-VNI description in the stem.

questions.question: Cisco BGP best-path selection is ORDERED — each tie-breaker only kicks in if the previous didn't decide. Which list correctly gives the FIRST three checks?
options: Origin code → MED → IGP metric to next-hop
AS-path length → Origin code → MED
Weight → Local Preference → Locally originated
Router ID → cluster-list length → AS-path length
questions.explanation: The canonical first three Cisco BGP best-path steps are Weight (Cisco-proprietary, router-local, higher wins), Local Preference (advertised inside the AS via iBGP, higher wins), and Locally originated routes (`network`, `aggregate`, `redistribute` are preferred over learned routes). AS-path length is the FOURTH check, after Locally originated. Origin code and MED come even later (steps 5 and 6). Router ID is the very last tie-breaker, used only when everything else is equal. The full mnemonic is 'We Love Oranges As Oranges Mean Pure Refreshment'.

questions.question: An MPLS SP wants to route GOLD-tier customer traffic along a specific path satisfying bandwidth + latency constraints, not just the IGP shortest path. The chosen technology signals LSPs with explicit-path + bandwidth requirements using RSVP-TE. Which feature is this?
options: LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) following IGP shortest path
BGP Labeled Unicast (RFC 8277) for inter-AS labels
Segment Routing over MPLS with default IGP shortest paths
MPLS Traffic Engineering signalled by RSVP-TE
questions.explanation: MPLS-TE uses RSVP-TE to signal LSPs with explicit paths and reserved bandwidth, allowing the operator to steer traffic around congested links even when the IGP shortest path traverses them. LDP only distributes labels along the IGP shortest path — it has no bandwidth reservation or explicit-path concept. BGP-LU distributes labels for prefixes between ASes but does not perform constraint-based routing. Segment Routing CAN do TE (SR-TE with PCEP), but plain SR-MPLS that just follows the IGP gives no bandwidth or latency constraint — and the stem specifically names RSVP-TE.

questions.question: An AS with 50 iBGP speakers naively needs 50×49/2 = 1225 iBGP sessions (full mesh) because iBGP routes are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers. Route Reflectors are deployed to scale this design. Which statement BEST describes when RRs are used?
options: Used to scale iBGP beyond an impractical n² full mesh
Mandatory whenever eBGP peers exchange routes
Useful only when BGP runs over IPv6 transport
Designed to replace BGP confederations entirely
questions.explanation: RRs sidestep the iBGP split-horizon rule by being explicitly permitted to re-advertise routes received from one client to other clients, so a partial mesh between RRs and clients replaces the n² full mesh. RRs are an iBGP-only construct — eBGP already re-advertises routes by default and never needs them. They have no relation to IPv4 versus IPv6 transport; both address families work the same. Confederations are an ALTERNATIVE iBGP-scaling design (splitting one AS into sub-ASes), not something RRs replace — most modern networks pick one or the other.

questions.question: An OSPF ABR sits between Area 0 and a non-backbone area. It learns Type 1/2 LSAs intra-area, then generates a SUMMARY LSA (carrying network + mask + metric) to advertise the prefix into OTHER areas. Receivers route by this metric. Which LSA type is generated and by whom?
options: Type 5 External LSA originated by an ASBR
Type 3 Summary LSA originated by an ABR
Type 1 Router LSA flooded only intra-area by every router
Type 7 NSSA External LSA originated inside an NSSA
questions.explanation: Type 3 Summary (Network) LSAs are originated by ABRs to advertise inter-area prefixes between Area 0 and non-backbone areas, carrying the destination network and the ABR's metric to it. Type 5 External LSAs are originated by ASBRs to flood external (redistributed) routes AS-wide and do not describe inter-area paths. Type 1 Router LSAs are flooded only inside one area and describe the originating router's links — never inter-area prefixes. Type 7 NSSA LSAs are confined to an NSSA and are converted to Type 5 at the NSSA's ABR, again not the inter-area summary role.

questions.question: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) has FOUR architectural roles. Which of the following mappings is correct for the SD-WAN management/orchestration plane?
options: vBond — initial onboarding and NAT traversal helper
vSmart — control-plane OMP route reflector
vManage — single-pane orchestration GUI and API
WAN-edge router — data-plane device carrying user traffic
questions.explanation: vManage is the management/orchestration plane — the single-pane GUI, REST API, and policy authoring point — exactly what the stem asks for. The other three are real Viptela components but different planes: vBond does initial onboarding/NAT traversal in the orchestration plane and ZTP, vSmart is the control-plane controller distributing OMP routes and policies to WAN-edge devices, and the WAN-edge routers (vEdge / cEdge / Catalyst 8000) form the data plane that carries user traffic across IPsec tunnels.

questions.question: Two link-state IGPs are compared: (A) OSPF runs over IP (protocol 89), uses Area-0 + non-backbone areas, and is IPv4-only in OSPFv2 (separate v3 for IPv6). (B) IS-IS uses single Level-1/Level-2 areas and one process for both AFs. Which statement BEST describes IS-IS?
options: IS-IS runs over UDP on the same port as RIP
IS-IS supports only OSI CLNS, never IPv4 or IPv6
IS-IS area boundaries follow the same /8 limit OSPF imposes on areas
IS-IS is a link-state IGP encapsulated directly in Layer-2 CLNS PDUs
questions.explanation: IS-IS PDUs ride directly on Layer 2 inside CLNS frames (ISO 10589), so the protocol is unreachable from an IP-spoofed remote attacker and is independent of IP version — multi-topology IS-IS carries IPv4 and IPv6 in one process. It does not run over UDP at all (that is RIP/EIGRP-IPv6). IS-IS does support IPv4 and IPv6 — the 'CLNS-only' description ignores the IPv4/IPv6 reachability TLVs that ISPs rely on. And IS-IS area numbers are area addresses in the NET, not the OSPF-style 32-bit IDs, so the OSPF /8 mask constraint does not apply.

questions.question: DMVPN has THREE phases. Which option BEST describes the differences between Phase 1, Phase 2 and Phase 3?
options: Phase 1 = hub-only; Phase 2 = NHRP spoke-to-spoke; Phase 3 = NHRP summarisation + redirects
Phase 1 = direct spoke-to-spoke; Phase 2 = hub-only; Phase 3 = static-tunnel IPsec replacement
All three phases keep the data plane on the hub indefinitely without spoke-to-spoke tunnels
Phase 2 deprecates GRE entirely and switches the DMVPN data plane to native IPsec only
questions.explanation: DMVPN Phase 1 is hub-and-spoke only — spokes cannot build direct tunnels and all traffic transits the hub. Phase 2 enables dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels via NHRP resolution: spoke A queries the hub for spoke B's NBMA address, then builds a direct mGRE+IPsec tunnel; the hub stays in the routing path for first packets. Phase 3 adds NHRP shortcut summarisation and Redirect messages so the data plane goes spoke-to-spoke immediately even when the hub is summarising routes. The other choices invert the phases, claim the hub stays in the data path (only true of Phase 1), or wrongly remove GRE (DMVPN keeps mGRE in every phase).

questions.question: QoS markings use the DSCP field. Which statement correctly identifies the DSCP field and well-known markings?
options: A 3-bit field identical to legacy IP Precedence, giving 8 marking values overall
A 6-bit field in the IP TOS byte; EF=46 for VoIP, CS6=48 for control
An MPLS EXP / Traffic-Class field that is used only inside the provider core
The 3-bit 802.1p CoS value that is carried in the 802.1Q tag at Layer 2
questions.explanation: DSCP occupies the upper 6 bits of the IP TOS/Traffic-Class byte (64 code points). EF (46) is the strict-priority VoIP marking, CS6 (48) is reserved for network control such as routing protocols, AF21–AF43 cover the assured-forwarding classes, and CS0 (0) is best-effort. The 3-bit IP-Precedence field is the LEGACY scheme that DSCP superseded (DSCP is fully backwards-compatible with the CS code points). MPLS EXP/TC is a separate 3-bit field in the MPLS shim header used inside an LSP, not in the IP header. 802.1p CoS is a Layer-2 marking in the VLAN tag — different layer, different field.

questions.question: An OSPF design has a non-backbone Area 5 attached only to Area 2 (no direct Area-0 link). OSPF rules require every non-backbone area to TOUCH Area 0. Which logical OSPF construct lets the area's ABR reach Area 0 across a transit area?
options: Configuring Area 5 as a stub area to block Type 5 LSAs
Building a GRE tunnel between the ABRs and running OSPF over it
An OSPF virtual link across the transit area to Area 0
Redistributing OSPF into BGP and back to glue the areas
questions.explanation: A virtual link is an OSPF-internal logical adjacency that runs across a non-stub transit area to repair a disconnected backbone, configured on both ABRs with the remote ABR's router-id. A stub-area declaration changes LSA filtering but does nothing to attach Area 5 to Area 0. A GRE tunnel with OSPF over it is a DATA-plane workaround that works in practice but is not the OSPF-native construct the question asks about (and it bypasses the OSPF rule rather than satisfying it). Redistributing into BGP loses OSPF-internal metrics and breaks the single-area model entirely.

questions.question: EIGRP's loop-free pre-computed alternative path requires the Feasibility Condition: a candidate's ADVERTISED DISTANCE (neighbour's metric to the destination) must be LESS than the current successor's FEASIBLE DISTANCE (my best metric). Which option correctly describes what passes this check?
options: The new successor route that DUAL recomputes after a topology change occurs
An equal-cost-multipath path installed by EIGRP variance for load balancing
Any neighbour's advertised route, usable only after an active-state DUAL query
A Feasible Successor: a pre-computed loop-free backup meeting AD<FD
questions.explanation: A Feasible Successor is a backup route whose advertised distance is strictly less than the local feasible distance, guaranteeing it cannot be a loop. EIGRP installs it instantly on successor failure with no DUAL query. The 'successor recomputed by DUAL' describes what happens AFTER a failure when no FS exists — DUAL goes active and queries neighbours. Variance-installed equal-cost paths are an unequal-cost load-balancing feature, unrelated to the FC. Calling any neighbour's route an FS misses the point: only routes satisfying AD<FD qualify, otherwise the route is just a possibility for the active-state query.

questions.question: A Cisco data-centre SDN solution is described: an APIC controller cluster, spine-leaf physical fabric, intent-based policy via Endpoint Groups (EPGs) and contracts, declarative model. Application teams define policies; the fabric enforces them across physical and virtual workloads. Which product?
options: Cisco ACI — APIC controller plus EPG/contract policy on Nexus spine-leaf
A link-state routing protocol designed for spine-leaf underlays
The VXLAN data-plane encapsulation standard itself
A campus wireless LAN controller architecture
questions.explanation: Cisco ACI is the only product that ships an APIC controller cluster managing a Nexus 9000 spine-leaf fabric with an EPG/contract policy model — that exact list is the definition of ACI. A link-state routing protocol such as IS-IS DOES run inside the ACI underlay, but the question describes the whole solution, not just the underlay IGP. VXLAN is the encapsulation ACI uses on the wire but is itself a standard, not a controller-based product. WLC architecture (Cisco 9800 / Catalyst Wireless) governs wireless campus, not data-centre east-west traffic and EPG policy.

questions.question: OSPF Hello = 10 s and BGP keepalive = 60 s are too slow for sub-second failover. A lightweight companion protocol exchanges very-frequent (e.g., 50 ms) Hellos between two endpoints and, on failure, instantly notifies the routing protocols to converge. Which protocol?
options: A first-hop redundancy protocol providing active/standby gateways
BFD — sub-second Hellos that signal OSPF/EIGRP/BGP to reconverge
A TCP keepalive tuning option specific to BGP sessions
An IGP that replaces OSPF specifically to deliver faster convergence
questions.explanation: BFD (RFC 5880) runs over UDP/3784, sends Hellos every 50–300 ms with a small detect-multiplier, and signals registered clients — OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, BGP and even static routes — the moment the session goes down. It must be enabled on both ends. An FHRP (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP) provides gateway redundancy on a LAN, not link-failure detection for IGPs. BGP TCP keepalive tuning lowers the BGP keepalive but does not help OSPF or static routes. There is no 'replacement IGP for fast convergence' — fast convergence is achieved by tuning timers and adding BFD, not by swapping the IGP.

questions.question: Two VXLAN data-plane modes exist. Which option correctly contrasts the FLOOD-AND-LEARN mode against the MP-BGP EVPN control-plane mode?
options: Both modes require underlay IP multicast to learn endpoints and reach the same scalability ceiling
EVPN floods BUM traffic across the underlay while flood-and-learn distributes MAC/IP bindings via BGP
Flood-and-learn relies on BUM flooding; EVPN advertises MAC/IP in BGP Type-2 routes
They are two names for the same VXLAN control-plane mechanism, just renamed by different vendors
questions.explanation: Flood-and-learn VXLAN discovers MACs the way classic Ethernet does — by flooding broadcast/unknown-unicast/multicast (BUM) across the underlay (multicast or ingress-replication) and learning source MACs on receipt. MP-BGP EVPN instead carries MAC and MAC/IP bindings in BGP Type-2 routes (and BUM membership in Type-3), so VTEPs know endpoints before any data arrives and no flooding is needed. The reverse claim swaps the two roles. BUM flooding is required only in flood-and-learn; EVPN with ARP suppression often avoids underlay multicast entirely. And the two modes have fundamentally different scaling and convergence properties — they are not the same mechanism.

questions.question: In BGP, a ROUTE LEAK is what condition? Multi-homed customers are a classic source; prevention uses prefix lists, AS-PATH filters and RPKI origin validation.
options: A physical fibre cut that withdraws prefixes from the table and depeers a session
An iBGP split-horizon forwarding loop contained entirely within a single AS
An RPKI origin-validation failure on an otherwise valid and legitimately announced route
Advertising routes received from one peer to another peer in violation of policy
questions.explanation: RFC 7908 defines a route leak as the propagation of a BGP announcement beyond its intended scope — typically a multi-homed customer re-advertising one upstream's routes to another and accidentally offering transit. Prevention is outbound prefix lists, AS-PATH filters, BGP communities and RPKI/ROA-based origin validation plus ASPA. A fibre cut withdraws prefixes via normal BGP UPDATEs (it is not a 'leak'). iBGP split-horizon prevents a class of intra-AS loops and has nothing to do with leaks between ASes. An RPKI-invalid origin is a different problem (the originating ASN doesn't match the ROA) — most operators reject those independently of any leak.

questions.question: An MPLS-enabled core has hundreds of LSRs forwarding by label-swapping. Each LSR must learn which label its peers use for a given FEC. Cisco runs a control protocol over TCP 646 to advertise label-to-FEC bindings between LSRs. Which protocol?
options: LDP — Label Distribution Protocol on TCP 646
RSVP-TE bandwidth reservation extension to RSVP
IS-IS Segment Routing (SR) labels distributed by the IGP
BGP Labeled Unicast (RFC 8277) for inter-AS labels
questions.explanation: LDP (RFC 5036) builds adjacencies between LSRs using UDP 646 multicast Hellos, then opens TCP 646 sessions to exchange label mappings for each FEC, populating the LFIB. RSVP-TE is the alternative label-distribution protocol used specifically for MPLS-TE with bandwidth reservations — it is not the default IGP-shortest-path distribution. SR-IS-IS distributes labels (SIDs) inside the IGP and avoids LDP entirely — it is a competing approach, not the protocol the stem describes. BGP-LU distributes labels for prefixes across AS boundaries (typically in Inter-AS MPLS Option C/Carriers-Carrier) — not between every pair of LSRs in a single core.

questions.question: Cisco's central intent-based controller for ENTERPRISE campus networks provides: design templates, provisioning to onboarded devices, ML-based assurance analytics, and group-based segmentation via SGTs. It was renamed Catalyst Center in 2024. Which product?
options: The APIC controller cluster that manages an ACI spine-leaf data-centre fabric
Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center) — intent-based enterprise management
vManage — the Cisco SD-WAN single-pane orchestrator for WAN-edge devices
Cisco ISE — the identity-services NAC policy and 802.1X authentication platform
questions.explanation: DNA Center / Catalyst Center automates campus lifecycle: design (IP plans, profiles), policy (SGTs and group-based ACLs), provisioning (PnP zero-touch and SWIM image management) and assurance (ML-driven Network Health and AI Endpoint Analytics). APIC manages an ACI data-centre fabric — different product, different domain (DC, not campus). vManage is the SD-WAN orchestrator that manages WAN-edge devices, not the campus access/distribution. ISE handles identity, 802.1X authentication and policy distribution, but the design/provision/assurance lifecycle for the campus belongs to DNA/Catalyst Center.

questions.question: A modern Cisco NetFlow variant lets the operator CHOOSE which packet fields are used as flow keys (e.g., src IP + dst IP + port + ToS + AS number) and which fields are collected (interfaces, byte counts, TCP flags, AS path). Operators tune flow caches per use-case. Which feature?
options: An SNMP poll of interface byte counters (IF-MIB)
A packet-capture feature that stores full payloads (EPC)
Flexible NetFlow — operator-defined keys and collected fields
Fixed five-tuple export with no operator customisation (classic NetFlow v5)
questions.explanation: Flexible NetFlow (FNF) replaced classic NetFlow's hard-coded record format with operator-defined Record/Exporter/Monitor pieces — pick the match (key) fields, the collect fields, the cache type and the exporter, then bind a monitor to an interface. SNMP polling of IF-MIB octet counters reports byte totals per interface but knows nothing about flows. Embedded Packet Capture stores entire payloads — useful for troubleshooting but not the per-flow metadata export the stem describes. Classic NetFlow v5 is the FIXED five-tuple format that FNF replaced; the question is specifically asking about the configurable version.

questions.question: Cisco TrustSec assigns a 16-bit GROUP TAG to each authenticated endpoint via ISE. The tag propagates with the packet inline (Cisco Metadata header) or via SXP, and policy enforcement compares src + dst tags at the egress device against a permissions matrix. Which architecture?
options: A site-to-site IPsec VPN technology between branch routers
A VLAN-based segmentation scheme using 802.1Q tags
A spanning-tree loop-prevention enhancement
Cisco TrustSec — SGT propagation plus SGACL enforcement
questions.explanation: TrustSec separates classification (assigning a Security Group Tag at the ingress edge via ISE) from enforcement (matching src/dst SGT pairs against an SGACL matrix at the egress). Tags travel inline in the Cisco Metadata header or over SXP between non-CMD-capable devices. IPsec site-to-site VPNs encrypt traffic between sites but do not implement identity-based policy. 802.1Q VLAN segmentation tags Layer-2 frames but ties identity to a port/VLAN, not to a user role — it scales badly and is what TrustSec replaces. Spanning-tree enhancements (BPDU Guard, Root Guard, Loop Guard) protect the L2 topology and have nothing to do with policy enforcement.

questions.question: In DMVPN Phase 2/3, a spoke wants to build a tunnel directly to another spoke. It must resolve the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a mapping table; spokes query it on demand via a specific protocol. Which?
options: NHRP — Next Hop Resolution Protocol; spokes query the hub for the peer's NBMA address
A routing protocol that advertises spoke prefixes to the hub (EIGRP/OSPF/BGP)
An IPsec key-exchange protocol used for tunnel setup (IKEv2)
A QoS marking mechanism applied to tunnel traffic
questions.explanation: NHRP (RFC 2332) is the 'phone book' of DMVPN: hubs act as Next-Hop Servers, spokes register their tunnel-to-NBMA mapping with the NHS, and on demand a spoke sends an NHRP Resolution Request to learn another spoke's NBMA address, then builds the direct mGRE/IPsec tunnel. An IGP/BGP advertises prefix reachability over the overlay but never carries the tunnel-IP-to-NBMA mapping. IKEv2 negotiates IPsec SA keys after the underlay reachability is already known — different layer. QoS marking influences forwarding behaviour but does not resolve anything.

questions.question: Cisco ships THREE distinct OS lineages for different roles. Which mapping is correct?
options: All three OS lineages share one image and differ only by licensing entitlements
IOS-XE on enterprise platforms; IOS-XR on SP edge; NX-OS on Nexus
IOS-XR is the modular campus OS while IOS-XE is the carrier-grade SP edge OS
NX-OS ships on ISR branch routers while IOS-XR ships on the Catalyst 9000 series
questions.explanation: IOS-XE is Cisco's modular Linux-based enterprise OS on ISR/ASR 1000/Catalyst 9000. IOS-XR is the carrier-grade microkernel/Linux OS for SP edge platforms (ASR 9000, NCS, CRS) with per-process restart and ISSU. NX-OS is the Nexus data-centre OS with VDCs, vPC, FabricPath/VXLAN-EVPN and NX-API. The 'same image, different license' claim is false — they are entirely separate code bases. The other reversals put each OS on the wrong platform family (XR on campus, NX-OS on ISRs) and would simply not boot on those devices.

questions.question: An LACP-bundled port-channel between two switches uses default LACP timers — PDUs every 30 s, partner failure detected in 90 s. The team wants FASTER member-failure detection. The LACP rate is changed from slow to fast. What does this do?
options: Adds bandwidth by activating standby member links in the bundle
Disables LACP and forces the bundle to static EtherChannel mode
Sends LACPDUs every 1 second and detects member failure in ~3 seconds
Changes the EtherChannel load-balancing hash to per-flow
questions.explanation: LACP rate fast sends LACPDUs every 1 s, so the standard 3× short-timeout means a missing partner is detected in ~3 s versus 90 s with default slow timers. The cost is a small increase in control traffic. It does not bring additional standby members online — that is `lacp max-bundle` plus hot-standby ports. It does not disable LACP — the static `channel-group X mode on` does that, removing PDU exchange entirely. And it has no effect on load-balancing; the hash algorithm is configured with `port-channel load-balance`.

questions.question: BGP allows tagging routes with 32-bit values that other ASes can match on to apply policy. Well-known examples include NO_EXPORT (don't advertise outside this AS), NO_ADVERTISE (don't tell any peer), and customer-tagged values like 65000:100. The values are transitive optional attributes. What is this feature?
options: 32-bit Autonomous System numbers used directly as a BGP best-path tie-breaker
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) values that influence a peer's inbound path selection
Local-preference values that are advertised across eBGP sessions to external peers
BGP communities — 32-bit tags such as NO_EXPORT and NO_ADVERTISE
questions.explanation: BGP communities (RFC 1997) are 32-bit transitive optional attributes attached to routes and matched by neighbouring ASes via route-maps to drive local policy (set local-pref, prepend, blackhole, etc.). Well-known values include NO_EXPORT (0xFFFFFF01), NO_ADVERTISE (0xFFFFFF02) and NO_EXPORT_SUBCONFED. 32-bit AS numbers (RFC 6793) are address-space, not policy tags. MED is a non-transitive metric carried in UPDATEs but is NOT a tag pattern like community:value. Local-preference is iBGP-only — it is dropped on eBGP advertisements, so it cannot be the inter-AS policy signal the question describes.

questions.question: OSPF can redistribute external routes (from EIGRP / BGP / static) into the OSPF domain in two metric flavours. Which option correctly contrasts E1 and E2?
options: E1 accumulates internal OSPF cost as it crosses the domain; E2 keeps the boundary cost fixed
E1 keeps a fixed cost at the boundary everywhere while E2 accumulates internal OSPF cost
E2 is used for intra-area redistribution and E1 is used for inter-area redistribution
Both E1 and E2 always select the same ASBR as the exit point regardless of internal cost
questions.explanation: OSPF external type 1 routes carry the ASBR's redistributed seed metric PLUS the cumulative internal OSPF cost to reach that ASBR — different OSPF routers therefore pick the closest ASBR. External type 2 (the default) keeps the boundary cost fixed everywhere; all OSPF routers see the same external cost regardless of how far the ASBR is, so the IGP tie-breaker is then forward-cost. The reverse claim swaps the two definitions. E1/E2 are not intra- versus inter-area types; both are external. And with E2, when multiple ASBRs advertise the same external prefix at different IGP distances, routers ROUTINELY pick different exits via the type-2 forward-cost tie-breaker — exits are not always the same.

questions.question: An enterprise NAC platform provides 802.1X with EAP, MAB for non-supplicant devices, device profiling from DHCP/HTTP/SNMP/active probes, posture assessment (AV / patch / config), and TrustSec SGT assignment. Which Cisco product?
options: A VPN concentrator that terminates IPsec tunnels at the edge
Cisco ISE — Identity Services Engine with 802.1X, MAB, profiling and posture
Cisco Umbrella — DNS-layer cloud security
Cisco Secure Network Analytics (Stealthwatch) for NetFlow-based detection
questions.explanation: Cisco ISE is the NAC/AAA platform combining a RADIUS/TACACS+ server with policy, profiling, posture and SGT-assignment services — every capability in the stem maps directly to an ISE feature. A VPN concentrator (ASA, FTD remote-access) terminates VPN tunnels but does not profile or posture endpoints. Umbrella enforces policy at the DNS layer in the cloud, not the network port. Stealthwatch consumes flow records to spot anomalous behaviour after authentication has already occurred — it does not perform 802.1X or assign SGTs.

questions.question: Cisco NSO is a MULTI-VENDOR orchestration platform with: YANG service models, NEDs (Network Element Drivers) translating service models to per-device configs, atomic network-wide commits, rollback, REST + CLI + Python APIs. Which option BEST describes NSO?
options: A Cisco-only campus SDN controller that manages SD-Access fabrics
A hardware spine switch used in Nexus 9000 ACI data-centre fabrics
Cisco NSO — multi-vendor orchestration via YANG models and NEDs
A flow-collector platform that ingests NetFlow/IPFIX for security analytics
questions.explanation: Network Services Orchestrator decouples a service intent (YANG service model) from per-device CLI/NETCONF/RESTCONF dialects via vendor-specific NEDs, and commits changes atomically across many devices with full rollback — exactly the role the stem describes. Calling it a single-vendor controller is wrong: NSO's selling point is multi-vendor (Cisco, Juniper, Nokia, Arista, …). It is software, not a hardware spine switch. And flow collectors (Stealthwatch, Splunk, ntopng) consume NetFlow/IPFIX for visibility — NSO is on the opposite side of the operations workflow: provisioning, not analytics.

questions.question: Network automation needs VENDOR-NEUTRAL DATA MODELS describing device configuration and operational state. The IETF picked a domain-specific modelling language with a human-readable, XML-Schema-like syntax. Models are used by NETCONF, RESTCONF and gNMI as the payload schema. Which language?
options: A Python automation library that wraps SSH connections to network devices (Netmiko)
An XML-over-SSH transport protocol that runs on TCP port 830 (NETCONF)
A CLI templating tool used to render IOS configuration snippets (Jinja2)
YANG — vendor-neutral data-modelling language (RFC 6020/7950)
questions.explanation: YANG (RFC 6020 / 7950) is the IETF data-modelling language for network configuration and state — modules define containers, lists, leafs and types that NETCONF/RESTCONF/gNMI encode and transport. Netmiko is a Python SSH library that wraps CLI sessions — it is a transport tool, not a modelling language. NETCONF on TCP 830 is the transport/RPC protocol that CARRIES YANG-modelled data; YANG defines the structure. Jinja2 templates render free-form strings (e.g., IOS CLI) and have no schema, validation or operational-state model.

questions.question: An OSPF ASBR redistributes EXTERNAL routes (from EIGRP / BGP / RIP / static) into the OSPF AS. These routes are flooded throughout the AS — across area boundaries — as a specific LSA type. Which?
options: Type 5 External LSA flooded AS-wide (except into stub/totally-stubby areas)
Type 3 Summary LSA generated by the ABR
Type 1 Router LSA flooded only intra-area
Type 7 NSSA External LSA that never leaves its own area unconverted
questions.explanation: Type 5 External LSAs are originated by ASBRs to flood redistributed external prefixes AS-wide; stub and totally-stubby areas block Type 5 (and Type 4) flooding, in which case the area depends on a default route from its ABR. Type 3 Summary LSAs carry inter-area OSPF-internal prefixes, not external routes. Type 1 Router LSAs describe a router's own links and never cross an area boundary. Type 7 NSSA External is the equivalent of Type 5 INSIDE an NSSA where Type 5 is forbidden; it is then converted to Type 5 at the NSSA ABR — so the unconverted form indeed does not leave the NSSA.

questions.question: Cisco's older SDN controller (APIC-EM) was deprecated in 2019. Its successor (now renamed Catalyst Center) extends to Intent-Based Networking: device design + provisioning + ML-driven assurance + group-based policy. Which statement is correct?
options: They are the same product with only a name change
APIC-EM's successor is DNA Center (now renamed Catalyst Center)
APIC-EM is the data-centre ACI controller for Nexus fabrics
DNA Center was deprecated in favour of APIC-EM
questions.explanation: APIC-EM was Cisco's first-generation campus SDN controller (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller — Enterprise Module) — it shipped IWAN and EasyQoS apps and was deprecated in 2019. DNA Center superseded it with SD-Access fabric management, Assurance analytics and full automation at scale; Cisco renamed it Catalyst Center in 2024. They are NOT the same product — the code base, UI and feature surface are entirely different. APIC-EM is unrelated to ACI: APIC (without -EM) is the ACI data-centre controller for Nexus 9000 fabrics. The succession runs APIC-EM → DNA Center → Catalyst Center, not the reverse.

questions.question: Two BGP policy tools are contrasted: (A) a simple ordered list that ONLY MATCHES IP prefixes plus a mask-length range (e.g., `permit 10.0.0.0/8 le 24`). (B) A powerful ordered-rule construct that can MATCH on AS-path, prefix, community, metric, neighbour, AND SET attributes (local-pref, MED, weight, community, next-hop). Which option correctly contrasts the two?
options: Both tools can match on AS-path or community and SET local-preference on routes
A prefix list is strictly more powerful than a route map and can SET any BGP attribute
Prefix list matches prefix/length only; route map matches many fields and SETs attributes
The two are interchangeable names for the same BGP filter construct in IOS-XE
questions.explanation: Prefix lists are a fast, ordered, deny-by-default match tool for IP prefixes with `le`/`ge` mask ranges — they cannot match anything except prefix and length, and they cannot SET anything. Route maps wrap match/set clauses and can match on AS-path, community, prefix-list, metric, neighbour and more, and SET local-preference, MED, weight, community, next-hop, etc. Saying both can set local-preference is wrong — only route maps can SET. The 'prefix list more powerful than route map' claim inverts reality. And calling them the same tool ignores both the matchable-attribute set and the set capability.

questions.question: Two OSPF routers on the same segment must DISCOVER each other and verify the neighbour is still alive. Periodic packets every 10 s (broadcast / P2P) carry router-id, area-id, Hello/Dead intervals, DR/BDR addresses, network mask and authentication. Adjacency requires both ends to agree on these. Which OSPF packet?
options: DBD packets that summarise the link-state database
LSU packets that carry LSAs during flooding
LSAck packets that acknowledge received LSAs
Hello packets — OSPF type 1, used for discovery and liveness
questions.explanation: OSPF Hello packets (OSPF type 1) are sent every 10 s on broadcast/P2P (30 s on NBMA) to 224.0.0.5 and carry the discovery/liveness fields the stem lists. Mismatched Hello/Dead, area, stub flag, mask or authentication blocks adjacency. DBDs are exchanged AFTER 2-Way to summarise the LSDB; they are not periodic. LSUs carry the LSAs themselves during full database synchronisation and incremental flooding — also not periodic Hellos. LSAcks confirm received LSAs and do not participate in neighbour discovery at all.

questions.question: Two tenants share ONE physical router but must have ISOLATED routing tables — including OVERLAPPING IP space (both use 10.0.0.0/8). The router provides per-tenant RIB / FIB / interfaces / routing-protocol instances inside one chassis. Which technology?
options: VRF — Virtual Routing and Forwarding with isolated per-tenant RIB/FIB
A VLAN trunk that separates broadcast domains at Layer 2 between tenants
A VXLAN overlay segment identifier (VNI) carried over a shared underlay
A hypervisor virtual switch such as the vSphere Distributed Switch (DVS)
questions.explanation: VRFs partition the routing table inside a single device: each VRF has its own RIB, FIB, interface bindings and routing-protocol process, so overlapping 10.0.0.0/8 across tenants is fine. They are the foundation of MPLS L3VPN PE routers, the management VRF, and per-tenant routing in SD-Access. A VLAN trunk separates broadcast domains at Layer 2 but does not produce isolated Layer-3 RIBs — multiple VLANs typically still feed one global routing table without VRFs. VXLAN VNIs are a data-plane Layer-2 segment identifier — they require VRFs (or a tenant routing instance) at L3 to provide overlapping IP isolation. A hypervisor vSwitch operates inside the host and is not a router feature at all.

questions.question: Branch users on roaming laptops need protection from malicious domains BEFORE the TCP connection is established. A cloud DNS resolver blocks lookups for known-bad domains, malware C2 and phishing sites — at the DNS layer. Which Cisco product?
options: A Cisco AnyConnect site-to-site IPsec VPN service
Cisco Umbrella — DNS-layer security with Talos threat intelligence
Cisco Secure Network Analytics (Stealthwatch) NetFlow-based detection
Cisco Firepower NGFW deployed on-premises at each branch
questions.explanation: Cisco Umbrella resolves DNS in the cloud, applies Talos threat intelligence to block malicious destinations BEFORE the TCP/TLS handshake, and follows roaming laptops with the Umbrella module in Secure Client/AnyConnect. AnyConnect VPNs back-haul traffic to corporate but do not themselves enforce DNS-layer policy. Stealthwatch consumes NetFlow to spot anomalies AFTER traffic has flowed — it is detection, not pre-connection blocking. A branch Firepower NGFW is on-premises hardware; it does not follow a roaming user once they leave the office network.

questions.question: A SecOps team wants behavioural anomaly detection across the network — insider threat, command-and-control, slow data exfiltration — by analysing NetFlow / IPFIX over time. The platform applies ML / behavioural baselines to flag anomalies. Which Cisco product?
options: Cisco Firepower NGFW operating inline as a stateful firewall
Cisco Umbrella — DNS-layer cloud security gateway
Cisco Secure Network Analytics (Stealthwatch) — ML over NetFlow/IPFIX
A packet-capture appliance that stores full payloads (e.g., Cisco SAS / EPC)
questions.explanation: Secure Network Analytics (formerly Stealthwatch) ingests NetFlow/IPFIX from existing routers, switches and firewalls and applies behavioural baselines plus ML to flag C2 beaconing, ransomware spread, slow data exfiltration and policy violations — agentless visibility that matches the stem exactly. A stateful firewall blocks inline at the perimeter but does not retro-analyse historical flow records for behaviour. Umbrella enforces at DNS, not by analysing flows. A packet-capture appliance stores full payloads for forensic replay; it does not provide behavioural anomaly scoring over flow metadata.

questions.question: Encrypted traffic can't be content-inspected without DECRYPTION (which is expensive and ethically contentious). A Cisco capability analyses metadata — packet-size patterns, TLS fingerprints, inter-packet timing, sequence of packet lengths — to detect malware C2 in TLS without decrypting. Which technology?
options: Encrypted Traffic Analytics — ML over flow metadata, no decryption
A TLS decryption proxy that inspects the cleartext payload
A certificate-pinning enforcement feature on the client
A QoS classifier that prioritises encrypted video flows
questions.explanation: Encrypted Traffic Analytics (ETA) was introduced on Catalyst 9000 and ISR/ASR platforms: it exports the Initial Data Packet (IDP) and Sequence of Packet Lengths and Times (SPLT) along with NetFlow, and Cisco's Cognitive analytics applies ML to spot malware C2 patterns in TLS without decrypting. A TLS decryption proxy (e.g., Firepower SSL inspection) DOES decrypt — the opposite of what the question asks. Certificate pinning is an application-side defence against rogue CAs, not a malware detector. QoS classifiers tag traffic for queuing/scheduling and have nothing to do with security analytics.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access architecture has two distinct planes. (Underlay) Traditional IP routing between fabric nodes — provides L3 connectivity for overlay tunnels. (Overlay) Tunnels carrying user traffic in segments/tenants. Which mapping is correct?
options: Underlay = routed IP (typically IS-IS); overlay = VXLAN with LISP control plane
Underlay = VXLAN tunnels carrying user traffic; overlay = the physical IP routing
Both planes share a single OSPF process for endpoint and underlay reachability
Overlay is the cabling and physical wiring while underlay carries user traffic
questions.explanation: SD-Access uses IS-IS in the underlay (routed access between fabric nodes) to provide loopback-to-loopback reachability, then builds a VXLAN overlay between fabric edges with LISP as the control plane for endpoint-to-edge mapping. The reverse assignment confuses encapsulation roles. Running a single OSPF process for both planes would tie endpoint mobility to IGP convergence and defeat the SD-Access design — neither plane is OSPF-only. And calling the overlay 'cabling' inverts the meaning of overlay/underlay: cabling is physical infrastructure, overlay is the logical tunnels on top.

questions.question: Traditional network segmentation uses VLANs / firewalls between SUBNETS / ZONES. Microsegmentation goes finer: policy is enforced between INDIVIDUAL WORKLOADS based on identity / role / tags — even within the same subnet. A compromised VM cannot freely talk to its neighbours. Which definition is correct?
options: Creating many very small IP subnets in the routing table to reduce broadcast scope
Per-workload policy by identity/role/tag, enforced within the same subnet
Placing every server behind its own dedicated physical firewall appliance
Encrypting all east-west traffic with IPsec or WireGuard between hosts
questions.explanation: Microsegmentation enforces policy between individual workloads using identity attributes (SGTs in SD-Access, EPGs/contracts in ACI, NSX DFW rules in VMware) — two workloads on the same VLAN can be blocked from each other if policy says so, which is the lateral-movement defence the stem describes. Slicing subnets smaller is just classic L3 segmentation — it does not move policy down to per-workload identity. Per-server physical firewalls is a hardware-cost fantasy that nobody actually deploys at scale; microsegmentation is a software policy concept. East-west IPsec gives confidentiality but does NOT decide who is allowed to talk to whom — encryption is not authorisation.

questions.question: An automation team replaces CLI screen-scraping with a STANDARDISED programmatic config protocol. Encoding: XML; transport: SSH on TCP 830; operations: `get-config`, `edit-config`, `commit`; supports candidate datastore, atomic commits and locks. Defined by RFC 6241. Which protocol?
options: RESTCONF (RFC 8040) — JSON or XML over HTTPS
Classic CLI screen-scraping driven by Expect/Netmiko
NETCONF (RFC 6241) — XML over SSH on TCP 830 with candidate datastore
gNMI — gRPC-based streaming telemetry and config over HTTP/2
questions.explanation: NETCONF (RFC 6241) is the XML-over-SSH/830 protocol with the candidate datastore, atomic `commit`, `lock`, `get-config` and `edit-config` operations the stem lists — `ncclient` is the common Python client. RESTCONF is a closely related IETF protocol (RFC 8040) but uses HTTP(S) with JSON/XML and exposes a REST API over the same YANG models — not the SSH/830 + XML answer here. CLI screen-scraping is the OPPOSITE of what the team is replacing. gNMI is Google's gRPC-based protocol — also a YANG-modelled config/telemetry path, but the transport, encoding and RFC reference do not match the stem.

questions.question: A developer writing YANG-based automation for Cisco devices needs to (a) BROWSE available YANG modules per platform, (b) GENERATE NETCONF / RESTCONF payloads from those models, (c) TEST RPCs against a live device. Cisco ships a developer web app dedicated to this. Which?
options: A physical network-management appliance shipped from the Cisco hardware lineup
pyang — a command-line YANG model compiler and schema validator
ncclient — the canonical Python NETCONF client library for scripts
Cisco YANG Suite — browse, build and test YANG RPCs in the browser
questions.explanation: Cisco YANG Suite (github.com/CiscoDevNet/yangsuite) is a browser-based developer tool that loads vendor YANG bundles, lets you compose NETCONF/RESTCONF/gNMI payloads from the tree, and replays them against a live device — exactly the (a)/(b)/(c) workflow the stem lists. A physical management appliance is not a developer dev-tool web app. pyang is a CLI YANG validator/compiler; useful for module hygiene but not for live RPC testing. ncclient is a Python LIBRARY that you import into scripts — no GUI, no per-platform module browser.
